headline: 3 things to check before choosing a health plan
author: Christy Bieber

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Christy Bieber1 min

Open enrollment provides the opportunity to buy or change a health care plan. Whether you’re signing up for an employer plan or one on the individual health insurance market, there are three things to check.

• Network size: Some plans require you to go in-network for covered services except in emergencies. Others offer more affordable care from in-network providers. Find out how large the network is and whether your preferred providers are in-network.

• Maximum out-of-pocket limit: This is the maximum you’ll have to pay each year for covered medical services. There are often separate limits for in-network versus out-of-network care. Know them both to understand your financial exposure.

• Deductible: This is the amount you pay out of pocket for covered services before your insurer covers the bills. There’s often a separate in-network and out-of-network deductible. Until you pay your deductible, your insurer won’t pay for most care except an annual exam and some preventive services.

Understanding these three things helps you see what care you can access and how much you’ll spend. Plans with higher deductibles and maximum out-of-pocket limits have lower premiums, but you should be aware of the trade-off that you may spend more on care throughout the year.
Executive producer of shows
Life Hax: My husband refuses to have Thanksgiving dinner with my family

This letter writer tells us that her husband (“Jim”) has a perfectly wonderful relationship with her family. Except for one thing that comes up around the holidays: He absolutely refuses to have Thanksgiving dinner with them.

Jim’s issue with these dinners is that the family eschews the bedrock of a traditional Thanksgiving meal: They don’t serve turkey. Instead, the family plates up beef wellington as their holiday main. This is a meal, our letter writer explains, that’s as traditional to their family as turkey is to most people.
So what is this letter writer to do? In this week’s episode of Life Hax, advice columnists Carolyn Hax and Shane O’Neill deeply disagree on what’s appropriate.
Shane suggests the couple could just bring turkey to share with her family. Carolyn says offering up food would be perfectly fine — if only it weren’t the main dish.
Per Carolyn: “Could your husband please lose his ever-loving mind over the mashed potatoes? Or a pie? Please?”
To hear more from Shane and Carolyn, follow the Life Hax show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts. If you have your own question to ask, email LifeHax@washpost.com.
Reporter covering travel
When to hit the road for the least-bad Thanksgiving traffic
When it comes to Thanksgiving road trips, the early bird should get the easiest ride.

Traffic congestion in areas around New York City, D.C. and Los Angeles is projected to more than double during early afternoon and early evening drives on certain days before and after the holiday, according to data from traffic analytics firm INRIX.
The best advice from road trip experts: Start driving in the morning to avoid peak traffic jams.

A forecast from AAA using data from INRIX said the busiest driving days are expected to be the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving and the Sunday and Monday after. On the holiday itself, expect “minimal traffic,” the forecast said.

On the far edges of the travel period — Nov. 24 and 30 — drivers should be on the road before 1 p.m. to avoid the worst stretches starting around 2 p.m. and lasting through early evening. On Nov. 25 and 27, it’s best to head out before noon. And on the weekend after Thanksgiving, get driving before 11 a.m. as the worst congestion is expected to start at noon and last until 8 or 9 p.m., depending on the day.
AAA expects 72.9 million people to travel by car at least 50 miles from home between the Tuesday before Thanksgiving and the Monday after the holiday.
Visual correspondent covering California and the Southwest
L.A. train heists net thieves more than $22 million in goods, feds say
The freight train was still clattering down the tracks when a masked man using a red Milwaukee angle grinder sawed through the lock of a shipping container filled with Nike Air Max sneakers.

By the time the crew filmed this heist in October 2024, it had already allegedly stolen more than $167,000 in Nike shoes in another train job. According to a federal indictment released Thursday, they were just getting started.

The Southern California crew is charged with breaking into more than 70 shipping containers over 31 months, stealing more than $22 million in electronics, tools, sneakers and other apparel to be sold on the black market.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement announcing the indictment. The 14 men were arrested Thursday and a federal grand jury charged each of them with one count of conspiracy, 14 counts of theft and two counts of violence against railroad carriers.

Federal prosecutors say the crew was led by Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, and included his father and two uncles. They allegedly identified trains hauling high-value cargo from overseas and were moving through Southern California rail yards headed to distribution centers out of state. The thieves allegedly climbed aboard and cut air hoses to trigger the emergency brakes at predetermined locations, where they loaded rental trucks and vans with stolen goods.

The indictment comes during concerns about rail heists around the country. According to the Association of American Railroads there were more than 75,000 thefts nationally last year with a 50 percent increase year over year. In Los Angeles, a string of thefts in 2022 left hundreds of boxes strewn on the tracks.
“The images looked like a Third World country,” Gov. Gavin Newsom told reporters at the time. “What you saw here in the last week is just not acceptable.”
Reporter covering Latin America from Mexico City
El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term that could keep him in power until 2033
El Salvador’s popular and ironfisted president, Nayib Bukele, formally registered his candidacy for a third term Thursday, setting the stage for elections in February that he is expected to win.

Since entering office in 2019, Bukele, 45, has found widespread support at home and from some quarters abroad for his aggressive crackdown on organized crime and a steep reduction in homicides. But he has been widely criticized for curtailing civil liberties, sweeping up alleged gang members without due process, repressing political dissent and dismantling democratic institutions.

He has successfully consolidated his power in what has become a de facto one-party state. Last year, Bukele’s allies in the legislature changed the country’s constitution to allow a president to serve an unlimited number of terms. If he wins next year’s elections, he would remain president until 2033.
Speaking before cheering crowds Thursday after registering his candidacy at the country’s electoral tribunal, Bukele said that “some international media say there isn’t democracy in El Salvador.”
“I tell them, no, no, no, there wasn’t democracy in El Salvador before,” he said.

Bukele is launching his candidacy as he pursues a gang battle abroad, in Haiti, where he has deployed about 2,500 Salvadoran troops after four Salvadoran aviation technicians went missing during a gang ambush while supporting a United Nations-backed international force. This week, large crowds poured into the streets in Haiti to praise and thank Bukele.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
Texas governor-elect and Trump agree to work together on border security
President Donald Trump said Friday that Democrats, including Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, have called about bipartisan immigration efforts and that he is open to the possibility.
“It was a very productive call,” Trump said at a White House news conference of his exchange with Hinojosa, adding, “I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune she called Trump last weekend to discuss border security and explain why Texans near Big Bend National Park prefer electronic monitoring to a wall.

“He understands my commitment to keeping a secure border,” said Hinojosa, who grew up on the border. “I reached out to him to make sure that he had a direct line to me, and it was a very positive conversation.”

On Thursday, Hinojosa met the state’s border sheriffs and told Fox News, “We need the federal government to put more resources along the border,” noting that Texas has spent $20 billion on border security, including GOP Gov. Greg Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, which she told The Washington Post last week she is reviewing to determine its legality. She told Fox that ICE’s violent interior immigration enforcement “needs to end.”
“We have had people killed in the streets,” she said. “I will not facilitate that. Even President Trump has acknowledged that has gone too far.”
Reporter covering national politics and breaking news
Hat had traveled too far into Fiona’s intestines to safely remove, zoo says

A necropsy on Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo who died Thursday, showed that a knit hat she had ingested had traveled so far into her intestines that there was no way to surgically remove it.
In a statement Friday, zoo officials said their veterinary staff “tried everything they could” after Fiona swallowed a knit hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat almost two weeks ago.
The hat made its way to the middle of Fiona’s small intestine, about 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines, zoo officials said.
There was no way to reach the hat with upper and lower endoscopy, and laparoscopic surgery was not possible, given where the hat was located, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.

“Open incision in a hippo that size — with an incision that’s that long — would have been a death sentence for her, so the only option we had was supportive care, and unfortunately it wasn’t enough for her,” Wenninger said in a video Friday.

Fiona’s unexpected death came as a shock to millions who had followed her journey since she was born six weeks premature in 2017. Since her death, mourners have been leaving flowers, cards and even watermelons — a special treat Fiona used to get on her birthday — at a makeshift memorial at the zoo.
